title: The trick is wanting to be wrong
hook: What if changing your mind felt like winning instead of losing?
author: Julia Galef
summary: A scout tries to see the terrain accurately. A soldier tries to defend a position. The distinction offers a useful way to catch motivated reasoning.
body: When we argue, we often behave as though our beliefs are territory to protect. We search for supportive evidence and find ingenious reasons to dismiss inconvenient facts.
Julia Galef proposes a different identity: the scout. The scout's reward is an increasingly accurate map of reality, even if that means admitting an earlier view was wrong.
This is not the same as having no convictions. It means choosing beliefs based on what the evidence supports and making updates less emotionally costly.
takeaways: Notice whether you're investigating a claim or defending it.
Ask what evidence would genuinely change your mind.
Treat a corrected belief as progress, not defeat.
nuance: This is a conceptual framework from a book, not a guarantee that people can eliminate bias by attitude alone.
application: Pick one opinion you hold strongly. Write down one observation that would make you less confident in it.

quiz.question: Which question best reflects a scout mindset?
choices: How do I prove my side is right?
What evidence could change my view?
Who agrees with me?
quiz.explanation: A scout searches for an accurate picture, including evidence that could overturn a favored belief.

slides.title: What if changing your mind meant winning?
slides.html: Most of us defend beliefs like soldiers. What changes when we approach them like scouts?

slides.title: Defend a position—or map reality?
slides.html: Galef uses two metaphors for how people approach uncertainty.

left.label: SOLDIER
left.title: Protect the belief
left.text: Look for arguments that support what you already think.

right.label: SCOUT
right.title: Map the terrain
right.text: Look for the evidence that makes your understanding more accurate.

slides.title: Three questions to ask yourself
slides.html: You do not need to abandon convictions to become more accurate.

slides.title: Test an opinion you care about
slides.html: Pick something you feel strongly about. Imagine encountering a fact that genuinely challenges it.

interaction.prompt: What would a scout do next?
interaction.answer: Specify what evidence would change your confidence, then examine it fairly—not just evidence favorable to your existing view.

slides.title: A mindset, not a magic trick
slides.html:
This is a conceptual framework from a book. Simply wanting to be open-minded does not guarantee freedom from motivated reasoning.

The practical takeaway: Make it easier to notice and update mistaken beliefs.

title: Being good with money is not just about math
hook: The financially optimal choice can be the wrong choice for a human being.
author: Morgan Housel
summary: Financial success depends on behavior, uncertainty and personal circumstances, not simply on knowing the right formulas.
body: Two people can see the same numbers and make very different decisions because their lived experiences with risk are different.

Housel emphasizes that staying in the game is often more valuable than squeezing out every possible return. Plans that look optimal on a spreadsheet can fail if they require a person to endure a level of volatility they cannot tolerate.
That shifts the question from 'What maximizes the expected outcome?' to 'What strategy can I realistically stick with?'
takeaways: A sustainable plan can outperform an optimal plan that you abandon.
Risk tolerance is personal and shaped by experience.
Room for error is a feature, not wasted efficiency.
nuance: These are themes of the book, not individualized financial advice or a claim that risk can be eliminated.
application: Think of a recent financial decision. Separate what was mathematically attractive from what you could comfortably sustain.

quiz.question: Why might a less aggressive plan be more effective over time?
choices: It always has a higher return
It may be easier to maintain through uncertainty
It eliminates losses
quiz.explanation: A plan that survives real behavior and difficult periods can be more useful than a theoretically optimal but unsustainable one.

title: Your environment is a silent decision-maker
hook: Changing what is easy to do can matter more than trying harder.
author: James Clear
summary: Habits are shaped by cues and friction. Designing an environment can make a desired behavior more likely without relying entirely on motivation.
body: An intention to read every evening is fragile if the book is hidden and the phone is always within reach.

A central idea in Atomic Habits is to make desired actions obvious and easy, and make unwanted ones less convenient. Moving the book to the pillow and charging the phone outside the bedroom changes the choice architecture.
The strategy works through repeated, ordinary moments rather than heroic acts of discipline.
takeaways: Make desired behaviors visible and low-friction.
Raise the friction of habits you want to reduce.
Small repeated actions can compound over time.
nuance: Environmental design helps but does not resolve every barrier to behavior change.
application: For one habit you want, change a single physical cue today instead of writing another goal.

quiz.question: Which intervention best uses environmental design?
choices: Promise to use more willpower
Put running shoes by the door
Set a more ambitious target
quiz.explanation: A visible cue lowers the friction for starting the desired behavior.

title: Why wandering can be a competitive advantage
hook: In messy domains, an indirect path can teach you more than an early straight line.
author: David Epstein
source_title: Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World
summary: Some complex, unpredictable fields reward broad exploration and transfer of ideas across disciplines, challenging the assumption that early specialization is always best.
body: Practice in a predictable environment lets people learn stable patterns. But many real-world problems are less regular: goals shift, feedback is ambiguous, and yesterday's rules may not hold tomorrow.
David Epstein argues that experience across multiple fields can help people build analogies and transfer useful strategies from one context to another.
The message is not that specialists are unnecessary. It is that breadth can be strategically valuable, especially when you do not yet know which problems matter most.
takeaways: Broad sampling can reveal unexpected interests and skills.
Analogies across fields can unlock unfamiliar problems.
Whether to specialize depends partly on how predictable the domain is.
nuance: The book advances an argument spanning many examples; it does not establish that generalists outperform specialists in every setting.
application: Ask which tool from an unrelated field might illuminate a stubborn problem you are working on.

quiz.question: Where might broad experience be especially useful?
choices: In changing, poorly structured problems
In every task without exception
Only in beginner-level work
quiz.explanation: Transfer and analogy can help when a domain has uncertain rules and unclear feedback.

title: One meeting can cost more than one hour
hook: Some work isn't divisible into neat calendar blocks.
author: Paul Graham
summary: A meeting that looks small on a manager's calendar may fragment the uninterrupted blocks a maker needs to do difficult work.
body: For people coordinating other people, hour-long blocks can be useful. A meeting fills a slot, and the day keeps moving.
Writing code, doing research or composing a complex argument often has a different rhythm. It can require hours of continuous attention and substantial ramp-up time.
Graham's point is that two working styles have different interruption costs. Grouping meetings together can protect deep-work periods without banning collaboration.
takeaways: Calendar time and cognitive cost are not equivalent.
Complex creation often benefits from large uninterrupted blocks.
Batch meetings to minimize fragmentation.
nuance: This is an essay and a useful mental model, not a controlled study quantifying meeting costs.
application: Try clustering meetings at one end of a day and protecting one long block for your hardest task.

quiz.question: What is the hidden cost of a mid-afternoon meeting for a maker?
choices: Only the meeting duration
Potentially fragmenting a long focus period
The cost of the meeting room
quiz.explanation: The disruption can prevent starting or sustaining cognitively demanding work.

title: Curiosity can be a research strategy
hook: Sometimes the interesting thing that seems like a distraction is the point.
author: Paul Graham
summary: Following genuine curiosity, exploring neglected questions and iterating on small experiments can help uncover consequential work.
body: An important problem is not always labeled important at the beginning. Sometimes it starts as a question that keeps bothering one person.
Paul Graham argues that doing great work often involves finding where your interests and abilities meet, approaching the frontier, noticing gaps and exploring them.
Instead of demanding a complete roadmap, a small prototype or experiment can reveal what the next step ought to be.
takeaways: Serious work can begin as a seemingly frivolous question.
Look for gaps and anomalies at the edge of what you know.
Try small experiments and let findings guide the next step.
nuance: The essay is practical reflection rather than a universal, experimentally validated recipe.
application: Write down one question you have been curious about but dismissing as unimportant. What is the smallest way to investigate it?

quiz.question: What might be a useful first move on an overlooked idea?
choices: Wait for a complete plan
Run a small experiment
Ignore it until it becomes popular
quiz.explanation: Small exploratory work gives feedback before committing to a large plan.

title: Changing a system's rules can beat tuning its numbers
hook: Some interventions move a dial; others rewrite what the dial does.
author: Donella Meadows
source_title: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
summary: In complex systems, changing feedback, information flows, goals or rules can be more consequential than changing a single numerical parameter.
body: Consider a system that repeatedly produces the same bad outcome. Increasing a budget or changing one threshold might help, but often leaves the basic behavior intact.
Donella Meadows proposes a hierarchy of places to intervene in systems. Parameters are relatively shallow interventions. Rules, goals and the mindsets behind them can be deeper ones.
The useful question becomes: What mechanism keeps reproducing the outcome? Changing that mechanism may matter more than treating each symptom.
takeaways: Look for feedback loops and incentives before adjusting parameters.
Information flows can be powerful intervention points.
System goals and rules shape recurring behavior.
nuance: Meadows explicitly presents her ranking as tentative and context dependent, not a mechanical formula.
application: Choose one recurring problem at work. Identify the feedback loop or incentive that keeps it alive.

quiz.question: Which change is usually deeper in Meadows' framing?
choices: Changing a threshold from 7 to 8
Changing the system's governing incentives
Renaming a dashboard
quiz.explanation: Rules and incentives can alter how the system behaves, not just its current operating point.

title: You may have fewer ordinary moments left than you think
kicker: An unsettling way to count time
hook: What if you counted future dinners with someone, not years left to live?
author: Tim Urban
summary: Because time with loved ones becomes less frequent as circumstances change, the number of future shared moments can be surprisingly limited.
body: We tend to imagine relationships as stretching across many future years. But the number of days we actually spend together can change dramatically after moving out, changing jobs or relocating.
Tim Urban uses simple visual arithmetic to reframe the question: how many visits, weekends or ordinary meals might remain?
The point is not to predict an exact count. It is to recognize that attention and proximity are decisions, and that 'someday' is not a neutral plan.
takeaways: Think in shared occasions, not only years.
Frequency of contact changes the time you actually have.
Priorities shape how much remaining time you share.
nuance: The numbers in the original essay are personal illustrations, not population-level forecasts.
application: Choose one person you'd like to see more. Put a specific visit or call on the calendar.

quiz.question: What does the 'tail end' reframe emphasize?
choices: Predicting your lifespan precisely
The number of actual future shared occasions
Avoiding all long-term plans
quiz.explanation: The essay measures relationship time in shared experiences, which may be much scarcer than years suggest.

title: Long context does not guarantee long memory
kicker: A blind spot in language models
hook: The same evidence can matter less depending on where it appears.
author: Nelson F. Liu et al.
source_title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
summary: In the studied long-context tasks, language-model performance often dropped when relevant information was placed in the middle rather than near the beginning or end.
body: A model can accept a long input without using every part equally well. Liu and colleagues evaluated question answering and key-value retrieval while varying where relevant evidence appeared.
They observed a recurring position effect: performance was often better when information was near the beginning or end of context and weaker when it was in the middle.
The work motivates testing not only whether a document fits in a context window, but whether a model reliably retrieves information from different locations within it.
takeaways: Context capacity and effective context use are distinct.
Evidence position can influence performance.
Long-context evaluations should test positional robustness.
nuance: This is a finding in the evaluated models and tasks; it should not be treated as an invariant law of all newer models.
application: When evaluating an agent, insert identical key facts at different transcript positions and measure answer stability.

quiz.question: What did the paper primarily show?
choices: Models cannot process long inputs
Information position can affect retrieval performance
All prompts must be short
quiz.explanation: Position-dependent performance was the key experimental observation.

slides.title: The middle can go missing
slides.html: A model can accept a very long document and still struggle to use relevant evidence buried inside it.

slides.title: Same evidence. Different location.
slides.html: In the evaluated tasks, changing where relevant information appeared often changed model performance.

left.label: BEGINNING OR END
left.title: Often easier
left.text: Relevant material near the edges was frequently used more reliably.

right.label: MIDDLE
right.title: Often harder
right.text: Performance often deteriorated when evidence was placed in the middle.

slides.title: Capacity isn't reliability
slides.html: The researchers varied the position of evidence in question answering and key–value retrieval tasks.

items.title: Keep the question
items.text: The information need stays the same.

items.title: Move the evidence
items.text: Place the useful fact at different positions.

slides.title: Would your agent pass this test?
slides.html: Imagine the same critical requirement appears early, in the middle, or late in a long coding-agent transcript.

interaction.answer: Hold the task and fact fixed, vary only its position, and measure the stability of the agent's answer or implementation.

slides.title: Don't overgeneralize the result
slides.html:
The study established a failure pattern in its evaluated models and tasks. It does not prove that every current model behaves identically.

Lesson: Test effective context use, not just context-window length.

title: Your acquaintances can connect entire worlds
kicker: The surprising value of weak ties
hook: The most useful new information may come from someone you barely know.
author: Mark S. Granovetter
summary: Weak social ties can bridge otherwise separate groups and carry information across communities in ways close relationships often cannot.
body: Close friends frequently know the same people and encounter overlapping information. An acquaintance may move in a different social circle.
Granovetter's influential network-theory paper explains why those weaker connections can bridge groups and help information, opportunities and influence travel through a society.
The insight is structural: a tie can be valuable not because it is emotionally close, but because it connects parts of a network that are otherwise distant.
takeaways: Strong ties often reinforce local cohesion.
Weak ties can bridge distinct communities.
Network position matters alongside relationship strength.
nuance: The paper develops a sociological theory; individual outcomes depend on context and cannot be guaranteed from any single weak tie.
application: Reach out to someone outside your usual professional or social circle and ask what they are learning.

quiz.question: Why can weak ties transmit novel information?
choices: Acquaintances always know more
They may connect less-overlapping networks
Close friends never share information
quiz.explanation: Bridges between communities can expose people to information outside their immediate circle.

title: Remembering is itself a form of learning
hook: A short quiz can strengthen memory more than another reread.
author: Henry L. Roediger III & Jeffrey D. Karpicke
source_title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
summary: In experiments using prose passages, retrieval practice improved delayed retention compared with repeated studying, even without feedback during the retrieval attempts.
body: Rereading a paragraph can feel fluent, but that feeling is not the same as being able to recover the idea later.

Roediger and Karpicke compared repeated studying with trying to recall studied material. On later tests after delays, retrieval practice improved retention relative to restudying in their experiments.
This provides a practical reason for a learning app to ask a thoughtful question after each idea, rather than simply offering endless content.
takeaways: Retrieving knowledge can improve its later accessibility.
Confidence from rereading can be misleading.
A brief recall attempt can be worth the added effort.
nuance: Study conditions, delay intervals and material type affect effect sizes; it is not true that testing always beats studying in every condition.
application: After reading an idea, close the article and explain it in one or two sentences from memory.

quiz.question: Why include a recall question after an insight?
choices: To make reading take longer
Retrieval practice may improve delayed retention
Because all quizzes are equally helpful
quiz.explanation: Trying to retrieve information is itself a learning activity, according to the testing-effect literature.

title: Why general methods keep beating clever handcrafting
hook: A method that scales with computation can eventually surpass one built from expert tricks.
author: Richard Sutton
summary: Sutton argues that AI approaches able to leverage increasing computation through general search and learning have historically outperformed domain-specific hand-engineered knowledge over the long run.
body: It is tempting to make an AI system stronger by encoding the human expert's hard-won knowledge directly into it.
Richard Sutton points to several historical episodes in AI where scalable general methods, especially search and learning, ultimately improved faster as compute became abundant.
The lesson is about long-run scaling trends, not a claim that domain expertise is useless in contemporary engineering.
takeaways: Scalability with compute can matter more than hand-tuned sophistication.
General learning and search methods transfer across domains.
Short-term engineering gains and long-term trends need not align.
nuance: This is an influential interpretive essay, not a theorem or a controlled meta-analysis of all AI systems.
application: In a system you're designing, identify which gains come from generic scaling and which require manual domain assumptions.

quiz.question: What is the essay's central historical claim?
choices: Expert rules are always best
General learning/search methods often gain more from scaling compute
Compute use should be minimized
quiz.explanation: The essay favors general methods that continue improving with available computation.

slides.title: Why the clever trick may lose
slides.html: Sutton argues that systems built around methods that scale with compute often win over hand-crafted expertise in the long run.

slides.title: Engineer knowledge—or learn at scale?
slides.html: The essay contrasts human-encoded solutions with general methods that improve as computing power grows.

left.label: DOMAIN-SPECIFIC
left.title: Hand-tuned rules
left.text: Good near-term performance can depend on many expert assumptions.

right.label: GENERAL METHODS
right.title: Search + learning
right.text: Performance can continue improving with additional computation.

slides.title: What scales can pull ahead
slides.html: The argument is about a recurring long-term trend, not a precise numeric law.

slides.title: What would you prioritize?
slides.html: You're building an agent and have a fixed engineering budget.

interaction.question: Where would you invest first?
choices: More bespoke task-specific heuristics
A general search/evaluation loop that improves with compute
interaction.feedback: Sutton's argument favors methods that can exploit more computation over time. That does not settle every short-term design trade-off.

slides.title: Expert knowledge still matters
slides.html:
This influential essay is an interpretation of AI history, not a theorem proving that handcrafted knowledge is never useful.

The question to ask: Which part of your system gets better simply by scaling search or learning?

title: The tiny winning network hiding in a big one
hook: What if a neural network has a much smaller version inside it that can learn just as well?
author: Jonathan Frankle & Michael Carbin
source_title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks
summary: In experiments on relatively small vision networks, researchers found sparse subnetworks that could train to comparable accuracy when their surviving weights were reset to their original initial values.
body: Training a large neural network can feel like searching through a vast number of possible connections. Could a much smaller network have succeeded from the very beginning?

Frankle and Carbin trained a dense model, pruned connections, then reset the surviving weights to their initial values before training the sparse network again. They repeated the process to find smaller subnetworks.

On MNIST and CIFAR-10 architectures, they found subnetworks with fewer than 10–20% of the original parameters that could achieve comparable accuracy. Their initialization mattered, not just the sparse structure.
takeaways: A dense network can contain smaller subnetworks with surprisingly strong learning behavior.
The specific initial weights can matter alongside the pattern of surviving connections.
Finding such a subnetwork retroactively is not the same as cheaply identifying it before training.
nuance: The original results focus on relatively small fully connected and convolutional vision networks. The winning tickets were discovered through training and pruning, not known for free at initialization; later work examined deeper networks and early-training rewinding.
application: When testing sparse networks, compare the original surviving initialization against randomly reinitializing the same sparse architecture.

quiz.question: Why did the authors reset the remaining weights to their original initialization?
choices: To show that any random sparse network learns equally well
To test whether the particular starting weights help the sparse network train
To increase the number of parameters
quiz.explanation: A winning ticket consists of a sparse connection pattern together with an advantageous initialization—not just a small network shape.

slides.title: A tiny winner hiding in a big network?
slides.html: Imagine a huge neural network. What if some of its connections already form a much smaller network that can learn just as well?

slides.title: A network inside a network
slides.html: The lottery ticket hypothesis says some randomly initialized dense networks contain smaller subnetworks with unusually favorable starting weights.

left.label: DENSE NETWORK
left.title: Many connections
left.text: Train the whole network, with lots of candidate paths.

right.label: WINNING TICKET
right.title: Few connections
right.text: Keep a special subset of connections and their original starting weights.

slides.title: Train. Prune. Rewind.
slides.html: They identified promising subnetworks after training the larger model—not by predicting the winners in advance.

items.title: Retrain
items.text: See whether the smaller net learns.

slides.title: Surprisingly small, still effective
slides.html: For several networks on MNIST and CIFAR-10, the authors found winning tickets with under 10–20% of the original parameters that reached comparable test accuracy. Some larger tickets even learned faster.

items.label: CAVEAT
items.title: Not free
items.text: Finding the ticket required training and pruning.

slides.title: Keep the connections, change the luck?
slides.html: You found a promising sparse subnetwork. Now imagine keeping the same connections but drawing fresh random starting weights.

interaction.prompt: Would the original result necessarily survive?
interaction.answer: No. The paper highlights the importance of the surviving weights' original initialization. The mask alone does not guarantee the same trainability.

slides.title: It's an insight, not a pruning shortcut
slides.html:
What it reveals: optimization depends on more than final model size; the starting point can help make a small subnetwork trainable.

What it doesn't prove: that we can cheaply identify winning tickets before training, or that every large modern model contains one at initialization.

title: A language model you can fit in your head
hook: What if you stripped a language model down until its entire learning recipe fit in one small Python file?
author: Andrej Karpathy
summary: Karpathy's microgpt is a deliberately tiny, dependency-free GPT implementation showing the core pieces of training and sampling in about 200 lines of Python; its toy output is names, not general intelligence.
body: Large language models can feel like an enormous stack of infrastructure. Karpathy's microgpt asks what remains when you strip away performance engineering and frameworks.

The small script loads a dataset of names, turns characters into tokens, builds gradients with a tiny autograd engine, trains a GPT-like transformer with an optimizer, then samples new names one token at a time.
The striking lesson is about conceptual simplicity, not capability: the core learning loop is compact, while modern model performance depends on scale, data, engineering, and much more.
takeaways: A minimal GPT training loop can be expressed in a small, readable program.
Training and generation are distinct phases connected by next-token prediction.
A toy demonstration is not evidence that frontier model capabilities are easy or cheap to reproduce.
nuance: microgpt is an educational implementation and personal essay, not a benchmarked research paper. Its scalar autograd and toy dataset are dramatically less efficient and capable than production systems.
application: When learning a complex ML system, separate the essential algorithm from engineering for speed, scale, and reliability.

quiz.question: What does microgpt primarily demonstrate?
choices: That a 200-line model can match frontier LLMs
That the core training and generation recipe can be implemented compactly
That tokenization and optimization are optional
quiz.explanation: It is a small educational implementation of the essential components, not a competitive large language model.

slides.title: Could GPT fit on one page?
slides.html:
Modern language models use vast infrastructure. But Karpathy's microgpt compresses the essential learning recipe into about 200 lines of plain Python.

The surprising part is how much machinery you can remove before the central idea disappears.

slides.title: Six ingredients, one tiny program
slides.html: It reads a list of names and learns to generate plausible new ones. The code includes the whole path from examples to samples.

items.label: INPUT
items.title: Data + tokens
items.text: Turn names into characters represented as numbers.

items.label: MODEL
items.title: GPT-like network
items.text: Predict the next token from previous ones.

items.label: LEARN
items.title: Gradients + optimizer
items.text: Adjust parameters to reduce prediction error.

items.label: OUTPUT
items.title: Sampling
items.text: Generate one new character at a time.

slides.title: Tiny algorithm, enormous engineering
slides.html: The demonstration is small because it sacrifices speed and capability. Real deployments add efficient tensor computation, massive datasets, distributed training, and careful evaluation.

left.label: MICROGPT
left.title: Understand the mechanism
left.text: A minimal educational model generating names.

right.label: PRODUCTION LLM
right.title: Scale the mechanism
right.text: Much larger systems with specialized optimization and infrastructure.

slides.title: What does it learn?
slides.html: After training on a dataset of names, the program samples new names one character at a time.

interaction.prompt: Does it memorize and replay only training names?
interaction.answer: Not necessarily. It learns a probability distribution over character sequences and can sample novel combinations that resemble the training examples.

slides.title: Simple does not mean easy
slides.html:
The insight: the conceptual core of language-model training is small enough to inspect.

The limitation: understanding the loop is not the same as reproducing the performance, safety, or cost of a modern LLM. This is an educational essay, not a new capability benchmark.

title: Your busiest day might not be your most productive
hook: A computer can tell you how long you were active. It cannot tell you whether you did valuable work.
author: Andrej Karpathy
summary: After tracking his own computer activity for nearly three months, Karpathy found useful discrepancies between time spent at work and time spent coding, while recognizing that activity traces do not measure productivity directly.
body: Karpathy built a local tool to log active windows and typing activity, then visualized nearly three months of his computer use.

He noticed that long days at the office could contain substantially fewer hours of coding than he had intuitively expected. He also saw patterns around deadlines, breaks, and applications, but treated possible explanations cautiously.
The larger lesson is about measurement: logs can challenge our stories about where time goes, yet typing and screen time remain imperfect proxies for creative or intellectual output.
takeaways: Observed activity can contradict our memory of how time was spent.
Time at a desk, typing intensity, and useful output are different quantities.
A measurement tool can create privacy risks and misleading incentives if used as a performance score.
nuance: This was one person's self-tracking project, not a controlled study. The logs missed activity on other machines and could not capture thinking, collaboration, or the value of finished work.
application: For one week, review broad time categories and compare them with actual completed outcomes—without equating keyboard activity with value.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of measuring productivity through active windows and keystrokes?
choices: It cannot measure any computer use
Activity is not the same as valuable output
It always overestimates coding time
quiz.explanation: Computer logs can reveal time allocation, but they do not establish the quality or importance of the work.

slides.title: Where did your workday go?
slides.html:
Have you ever spent all day at your desk and wondered what actually got done?

Karpathy built a tool to record his own computer activity and inspect the gap between how work feels and how time is spent.

slides.title: From vague memory to a timeline
slides.html: His local tracker recorded active windows and typing frequency, then turned nearly three months of activity into visual timelines.

items.title: Observe
items.text: Record active apps and typing activity.

items.title: Visualize
items.text: See how a day is divided.

items.title: Question
items.text: Compare the timeline with your memory.

slides.title: A long day isn't all deep work
slides.html:
He found that even days spent at the office from morning to night could contain only about five or six hours of coding.

Meals, meetings, browsing, and other work filled the rest. That's an observation about his own logs, not a universal productivity benchmark.

slides.title: What you can count isn't always what counts
slides.html: A typing-heavy day can be unproductive. A quiet afternoon of thinking might unlock the whole project.

slides.title: What would you measure?
slides.html: Imagine your calendar shows eight hours of work, but your keyboard tracker shows two hours of typing.

interaction.prompt: Can you conclude the day was unproductive?
interaction.answer: No. The logs reveal activity patterns, not the value of meetings, design thinking, reading, or decisions. Pair time data with meaningful outcomes.

slides.title: Use the mirror, not the scoreboard
slides.html:
This was a personal experiment with missing data and no causal proof. Tracking can also be invasive.

A useful practice: review where your time went, then ask what mattered—not how many keys you pressed.

title: Can a smell remind your sleeping brain?
hook: A scent present while learning may help the brain revisit that memory during deep sleep.
author: Julia S. Rihm, Susanne Diekelmann, Jan Born & Björn Rasch
source_title: Reactivating Memories during Sleep by Odors: Odor Specificity and Associated Changes in Sleep Oscillations
summary: In a controlled visuospatial-memory experiment, replaying the same odor during slow-wave sleep improved later memory compared with a different odor or odorless control; EEG changes accompanied the effect.
body: Our brains do not simply switch off learning during sleep. Researchers can sometimes cue recently learned memories with a sensory reminder.
Participants learned a visuospatial memory task in the presence of an odor. During subsequent slow-wave sleep, the researchers presented the same odor, a different odor, or an odorless control.

Only the matching odor significantly improved later memory in this experiment, accompanied by changes in sleep-related brain rhythms. That is a specific laboratory finding, not a proven everyday study hack.
takeaways: A cue can help reactivate a recently formed memory during slow-wave sleep.
The identity of the cue mattered: a new odor was not equivalent to the original one.
This is evidence about a controlled memory task, not a general recipe for overnight learning.
nuance: The experiment used a particular visuospatial task, controlled odor presentation and monitored slow-wave sleep. It does not show that arbitrary scents, sleep stages or new information can reliably improve learning at home.
application: When encountering claims about learning during sleep, ask whether the experiment replayed a cue linked to prior learning or attempted to teach entirely new material.

quiz.question: Which odor helped memory in the study?
choices: Any strong odor during sleep
The same odor paired with learning
A completely new odor
quiz.explanation: The effect was cue-specific: only the matching odor improved recall in the reported experiment.

slides.title: Could a smell wake up a memory—without waking you?
slides.html:
Imagine studying a pattern while smelling lemon. Later, as you sleep, that scent returns. Could it nudge your brain to revisit what you learned?

Researchers tested a controlled version of this idea.

slides.title: A reminder during deep sleep
slides.html: Participants learned a visuospatial task with an odor present. During later slow-wave sleep, researchers delivered a matching odor, a different odor, or an odorless control.

items.title: Cue
items.text: Present a matching, different, or absent scent.

slides.title: The right smell mattered
slides.html: The matching odor improved later memory in this experiment. A different odor did not produce the same benefit. The researchers also observed changes in brain rhythms associated with slow-wave sleep.

left.label: MATCHED
left.title: Same odor
left.text: Improved later recall in the tested task.

right.label: NOT MATCHED
right.title: Different or no odor
right.text: No comparable benefit in this experiment.

slides.title: Is this learning in your sleep?
slides.html: The participants had already studied the information before sleeping. The odor was a reminder, not a new lesson.

interaction.prompt: What did the scent actually do?
interaction.answer: It likely helped reactivate a memory linked to prior learning. The experiment did not show that new facts can be taught to a sleeping person.

slides.title: A laboratory effect, not a magic perfume
slides.html:
The study used a specific task and precisely timed odor delivery during monitored slow-wave sleep. We should not assume that spraying a room with a familiar scent will reliably boost everyday studying.

The interesting idea: a sleeping brain can remain sensitive to reminders of what it learned.

title: Four small debates can outguess a giant crowd
hook: Independent guesses are powerful—but a little structured conversation can sometimes make them better.
author: Joaquin Navajas, Tamara Niella, Gerry Garbulsky, Bahador Bahrami & Mariano Sigman
source_title: Aggregated knowledge from a small number of debates outperforms the wisdom of large crowds
summary: In a live general-knowledge estimation study with 5,180 participants, aggregating consensus answers from small independent discussion groups was more accurate than averaging initial individual guesses; even four group consensuses outperformed the large initial crowd in the reported setup.
body: The classic wisdom-of-crowds idea says averaging many independent estimates can cancel individual errors. But what happens if people talk first?
In a study with 5,180 people, participants estimated answers individually, discussed in groups of five, and produced group consensus estimates.

Averaging the small-group consensus estimates improved accuracy over the initial independent crowd. In the studied questions, just four group consensus answers outperformed aggregation of thousands of original guesses.
takeaways: Independence can help crowds, but discussion need not always destroy accuracy.
Small groups can exchange useful reasoning before their conclusions are aggregated.
The structure of deliberation and aggregation matters as much as the number of voices.
nuance: These results concern numerical general-knowledge estimates in a specific experimental setting. Groupthink, unequal influence, shared bias or different tasks can reverse the benefit; four groups are not universally better than thousands of people.
application: For a hard estimation question, first collect independent guesses, then let small separate groups deliberate, and aggregate their final estimates.

quiz.question: What did the researchers aggregate to obtain especially accurate estimates?
choices: Only the loudest individual's answer
Consensus estimates from separate small groups
A single giant-group discussion
quiz.explanation: The study combined multiple small groups' consensus estimates rather than relying on one large conversation.

slides.title: What if four tiny groups beat thousands of guesses?
slides.html: Everyone knows that crowds can be wise when their errors cancel out. But here's a twist: talking in small groups can sometimes make the crowd even wiser.

slides.title: First guess alone. Then discuss.
slides.html: In a live study involving 5,180 participants, people answered general-knowledge estimation questions individually, discussed in groups of five, and reached group consensus answers.

slides.title: A few conversations went a long way
slides.html: Combining small-group consensus answers beat aggregating the initial individual guesses. In this study, as few as four group consensuses outperformed the initial estimates of thousands of participants.

right.label: DELIBERATING GROUPS
right.title: Four consensuses
right.text: Combine answers after separate small-group debates.

slides.title: How would you organize a forecast?
slides.html: You want a team to estimate something uncertain. Should everyone immediately discuss in one giant room?

interaction.prompt: What alternative does this study suggest?
interaction.answer: Gather initial independent estimates, then let separate small groups debate and aggregate their consensuses. The study supports this on its tested estimation questions, not as a universal rule.

slides.title: Conversation can help—or hurt
slides.html:
The results do not imply that any discussion improves decisions. Strong personalities, shared misinformation and groupthink can still distort judgments.

The useful distinction: deliberate within small groups, preserve independence across groups, then combine what they conclude.

title: You understand a bicycle—until you explain it
hook: Why can familiar machines become mysterious the moment you try explaining how they work?
author: Leonid Rozenblit & Frank Keil
source_title: The misunderstood limits of folk science: an illusion of explanatory depth
summary: Across experiments, people often overestimated how deeply they understood everyday mechanisms; attempting a detailed explanation revealed gaps in their causal knowledge.
body: Being familiar with a device is not the same as understanding how its parts cause it to work.
Rozenblit and Keil studied people's judgments about their knowledge of familiar mechanisms, and found that asking for detailed explanations exposed surprising gaps.
The effect is particularly pronounced for explanatory knowledge, compared with some other forms of knowledge.
takeaways: Recognizing a mechanism is different from explaining its causal steps.
A detailed explanation can reveal hidden gaps in understanding.
Knowing where to find an explanation can feel like possessing it.
nuance: The experiments studied particular explanatory judgments and knowledge domains. The results do not imply that people know nothing, or that all confidence is misplaced.
application: Choose a familiar object, rate your understanding, then explain every causal step without looking anything up. Re-rate your confidence afterward.

quiz.question: What best reveals the illusion of explanatory depth?
choices: Recognizing an object's name
Trying to explain precisely how it works
Reading its price tag
quiz.explanation: Detailed causal explanation makes missing links visible, even when the object feels familiar.

slides.title: You know how it works. Right?
slides.html:
You use zippers, toilets, bicycles and locks without thinking. But could you explain, step by step, how each one actually works?

Researchers found that our sense of understanding can run well ahead of the details we can explain.

slides.title: Familiarity masquerades as knowledge
slides.html: We see the finished machine working and can usually operate it. That smooth experience makes it easy to confuse using a mechanism with explaining it.

left.label: FAMILIARITY
left.title: I know this
left.text: I can recognize it and use it.

right.label: EXPLANATION
right.title: I can trace why
right.text: I can connect each component to its effect.

slides.title: Ask for the gears, not the gist
slides.html:
Rozenblit and Keil asked people to assess their understanding of everyday mechanisms and then produce detailed explanations. The attempt exposed gaps that initial confidence had concealed.

Their broader studies found this illusion especially strong for causal explanations, rather than all kinds of knowledge equally.

slides.title: Explain a zipper
slides.html: Before revealing the answer, mentally describe exactly how moving the slider joins two rows of teeth. Where does each tooth go?

interaction.prompt: What does the slider actually do?
interaction.answer: Its shaped channels guide the two rows of teeth together so their profiles interlock; moving the other way separates the interlocked rows. Could you have explained the geometry before reading this?

slides.title: An explanation is a stress test
slides.html:
Before claiming you understand something, try teaching it from first principles. Wherever you have to say and then somehow, you have found a promising question.

But don't overcorrect: everyday competence is real, even without a complete mechanical theory.

title: Messy examples can beat elegant rules
hook: Why might a mountain of imperfect examples outperform a beautifully hand-built theory of language?
author: Alon Halevy, Peter Norvig & Fernando Pereira
summary: Halevy, Norvig and Pereira argue that for messy human domains like language, exploiting abundant real-world data can be more productive than trying to encode all the rules by hand.
body: Human language is full of exceptions, context and ambiguity. Compact hand-written rules struggle to capture that richness.
The authors point to statistical approaches and web-scale corpora as a practical way to learn recurring patterns from real behavior.
This is a perspective essay supported by examples from language technology, not a controlled proof that more data always wins.
takeaways: Complex human phenomena may resist compact handcrafted rules.
Large, imperfect datasets can capture rare patterns absent from curated samples.
More data does not automatically fix bias, poor measurement or evaluation.
nuance: Published in 2009, this is an argument from a particular era of data-driven AI. Its examples do not establish that data quantity always beats model quality, clean labels, or sound experimental design.
application: When a handcrafted rule system stalls, ask whether representative examples could expose exceptions you have not modeled—and test both approaches on held-out cases.

quiz.question: What is the central claim of the essay?
choices: All data should be trusted without cleaning
Real-world data can reveal patterns too complex to encode by hand
Language follows a small set of perfect rules
quiz.explanation: The authors favor learning from plentiful real-world examples for complex human-centered tasks, not blindly trusting any dataset.

slides.title: What if the messy answer is better?
slides.html:
Imagine trying to write every rule of human language by hand. Every exception. Every odd phrase. Every context.

Now imagine learning patterns from a vast collection of how people actually speak and write.

slides.title: Rules versus examples
slides.html: Halevy, Norvig and Pereira argued that domains shaped by human behavior may be too irregular for neat, compact theories to do all the work.

left.label: HANDCRAFTED
left.title: Specify the rules
left.text: Experts encode grammar, exceptions and cases.

right.label: DATA-DRIVEN
right.title: Learn from usage
right.text: Statistical methods infer recurring patterns from examples.

slides.title: Rare things stop being invisible
slides.html:
A small, carefully curated language corpus may miss unusual expressions entirely. A much larger, noisier corpus can contain examples of those rare patterns.

The authors highlighted how rapidly growing web data changed what statistical language systems could learn.

slides.title: More examples, more responsibility
slides.html: The essay makes a case for exploiting available data, not for assuming that every extra example helps. Sampling, bias, quality and evaluation still matter.

slides.title: Where would examples help?
slides.html: Suppose you're building a system to interpret slang that changes every year. Would you rely only on a fixed dictionary or also examine how people currently use words?

interaction.answer: Fresh, representative usage examples can reveal meanings that fixed rules miss. But they must be evaluated carefully: popular usage can still be biased or misleading.

title: You can look straight at something and miss it
hook: How can a person in a gorilla suit cross your field of view without entering your awareness?
author: Daniel J. Simons & Christopher F. Chabris
source_title: Gorillas in Our Midst: Sustained Inattentional Blindness for Dynamic Events
summary: In experiments with people monitoring basketball passes, many missed an unexpected person walking through the scene. What we notice depends on the task occupying our attention, not merely on what enters our eyes.
body: Participants watched videos of people passing basketballs and counted passes by one team. During the action, an unexpected person crossed the scene.
Many participants failed to report the unexpected event. Detection depended on the primary task's difficulty and the unexpected object's similarity to the attended group.
The study demonstrates inattentional blindness in a specific laboratory setup, not that attention makes us universally oblivious.
takeaways: Looking at a scene is not the same as noticing every event in it.
The task you are performing can shape which surprising details reach awareness.
Use independent checks when missing something would matter.
nuance: The precise rate of missed events varied with experimental conditions. This is a laboratory attention effect, not a claim that all observers miss a gorilla or that perception is always unreliable.
application: When reviewing a complicated document, do one pass for your main question and another for unexpected inconsistencies rather than expecting one focused pass to catch everything.

quiz.question: Why did some viewers miss the unexpected person?
choices: Their eyes could not receive the image
Attention was occupied by the counting task
The unexpected person was digitally hidden
quiz.explanation: The unexpected event was visible, but selective attention made it less likely to be noticed.

slides.title: The obvious thing nobody saw
slides.html:
Imagine watching a basketball game and counting passes by the team in white.

Someone in a gorilla suit walks through the scene. Would you notice? In a famous experiment, many people did not.

slides.title: Two things happen at once
slides.html: Simons and Chabris asked participants to track passes in a short video. An unexpected person entered the action while viewers concentrated on the assigned task.

left.label: YOUR TASK
left.title: Count the passes
left.text: Follow one team and keep a running total.

right.label: THE SURPRISE
right.title: Someone crosses
right.text: An unexpected person moves through the same scene.

slides.title: Seeing is not the same as noticing
slides.html:
Many viewers missed the unexpected event. Noticing varied with how demanding the counting task was and how similar the unexpected person looked to the attended players.

The point is not that eyes failed. Attention selected which parts of a busy scene reached awareness.

slides.title: What else might be invisible?
slides.html: Suppose you proofread a report only for spelling errors. Could you overlook a glaringly inconsistent number?

interaction.answer: A narrow task can direct attention away from other conspicuous details. A second pass with a different goal may catch what the first missed.

slides.title: Not a universal blindness switch
slides.html:
The researchers studied specific videos and attention tasks. They did not show that everyone misses the same event or that attention always blocks surprises.

Practical lesson: when stakes are high, use multiple review passes with different goals. A single careful look may still be selective.

title: An untrained neural network can help repair a photo
kicker: The architecture is already a clue
hook: What if the shape of a neural network—not a giant training dataset—helps recover a damaged image?
author: Dmitry Ulyanov, Andrea Vedaldi & Victor Lempitsky
summary: Deep Image Prior showed that the structure of a randomly initialized convolutional generator can be useful for restoring a single corrupted image. Fitting the network to that image can recover plausible structure without training on a separate image dataset.
body: The usual recipe for image restoration trains on many example images. Deep Image Prior instead begins with a randomly initialized generator and optimizes it for one corrupted image.
The generator's architecture favors some image structures over others, providing an implicit prior even before learning from a dataset.
The authors demonstrated denoising, inpainting and super-resolution on tested images. The network is still optimized per image, and stopping at the right time matters for denoising.
takeaways: Architecture itself can impose useful biases on possible outputs.
A neural network need not be pretrained on a large dataset to help with some image restoration tasks.
The method still optimizes weights on the target image; it is not instant restoration by random weights alone.
nuance: The 2018 experiments concern selected low-level image restoration problems, not general visual understanding. The method may eventually fit noise too; early stopping and task-specific settings matter, and it does not universally outperform pretrained restoration models.
application: When evaluating an ML method, ask which part of its success comes from learned data and which comes from architecture, optimization and other built-in assumptions.

quiz.question: What is surprising about Deep Image Prior?
choices: It restores any photo without any optimization
A network's architecture can aid restoration without prior dataset training
It requires millions of labeled photos to restore one
quiz.explanation: The randomly initialized generator is optimized on the target image; its architecture provides a useful implicit bias.

slides.title: Can a neural network repair a photo without a training dataset?
slides.html:
Most image-restoration systems learn from thousands of examples. But what if you start with a neural network whose weights are random?

Deep Image Prior found that even this seemingly clueless network can help reconstruct a damaged image.

slides.title: What comes from data—and what comes from design?
slides.html: Instead of learning from a collection of clean photos, the method adjusts one randomly initialized generator to reproduce a single damaged image.

left.label: FAMILIAR ROUTE
left.title: Train on many images
left.text: Learn restoration patterns from a dataset.

right.label: DEEP IMAGE PRIOR
right.title: Optimize for one image
right.text: Start random; use network structure as a built-in bias.

slides.title: Fit a generator, not individual pixels
slides.html: The network receives a fixed random input and produces an image. Its weights are adjusted so that the output matches the available corrupted observation, with a task-appropriate loss.

items.title: Random input
items.text: Feed a fixed noise pattern into a generator.

items.title: Fit
items.text: Adjust weights against the damaged observation.

slides.title: The structure itself helps
slides.html:
Ulyanov and colleagues demonstrated restoration on denoising, missing-region filling and super-resolution tasks. A convolutional generator tends to express useful image structure through its architecture, even without pretraining on an image collection.

That is an inductive bias: the model's design favors some solutions before seeing data.

slides.title: Could it eventually learn the noise?
slides.html: For denoising, optimizing forever is not necessarily wise. A sufficiently flexible network can eventually reproduce unwanted noise as well as image structure.

interaction.question: What might help preserve a cleaner reconstruction?
choices: Stop optimization at an appropriate point
Always optimize until every noisy pixel matches perfectly
Replace the image with unrelated training examples
interaction.feedback: Early stopping can matter: fitting the observation too closely may also fit noise.

slides.title: Not magic, not zero computation
slides.html:
The network still learns weights while fitting each target image. The result does not mean random weights alone restore photos, or that this method beats every pretrained model.

Its deeper lesson: performance can come partly from the architecture's assumptions, not just from information learned across a dataset.

title: Your future self is probably less fixed than you think
hook: You know you've changed. Why does tomorrow's version of you seem so permanent?
author: Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel T. Gilbert & Timothy D. Wilson
summary: In a study of more than 19,000 adults, people described substantial changes in their past personalities, values and preferences but predicted comparatively little change ahead. The contrast suggests we may underestimate how different our future selves will be.
body: Researchers asked adults aged 18 to 68 how much they had changed over the previous decade or expected to change over the next one.
Across ages, retrospective reports of change were larger than forecasts of future change, for personality, values and preferences.
This was largely a comparison between different people's recollections and forecasts, not a ten-year follow-up of each participant.
takeaways: Present preferences can feel more permanent than they really are.
Past changes offer a useful prompt when making long commitments.
The study measures reported change and predictions, not a perfect objective record of future personality.
nuance: The original design compared retrospective reports with prospective forecasts from different people, leaving room for memory, cohort and measurement effects. The pattern is not a law that every individual must change dramatically.
application: Before a costly commitment based on a current passion, ask what you cared about ten years ago and how easily your next decade could surprise you.

quiz.question: What did the original end-of-history study find?
choices: People reported more past change than they expected future change
People correctly forecast all future preferences
Personality stopped changing after age 30
quiz.explanation: Across ages, people described substantial past changes but anticipated relatively little future change.

slides.title: Are you already the final version of yourself?
slides.html:
Think about your favorite music, goals, or friendships ten years ago. Some probably changed.

Now picture yourself ten years from today. Oddly, that future person may feel much more like today's you than your past self does.

slides.title: We remember change, but predict stability
slides.html:
In a 2013 study involving more than 19,000 adults aged 18 to 68, researchers compared reports of past change with expectations of future change in personality, values and preferences.

At different ages, people described more change behind them than they expected ahead.

left.label: LOOKING BACK
left.title: I've changed a lot
left.text: Past tastes and values feel noticeably different.

right.label: LOOKING FORWARD
right.title: I'm mostly settled
right.text: Current tastes and values feel enduring.

slides.title: Today's preferences feel unusually final
slides.html:
The authors called this the end-of-history illusion: treating the present as if personal development has nearly finished.

That can matter when paying today for a future experience or making commitments based on what you currently love. A future you may want something else.

slides.title: Ask two versions of yourself
slides.html: Pick something you feel sure you will enjoy in ten years: a hobby, a city, or a kind of work. Now remember a strong preference from ten years ago.

interaction.prompt: What is the useful question to ask before a long commitment?
interaction.answer: What evidence do I have that this preference is more permanent than the ones I outgrew?

slides.title: A comparison, not a crystal ball
slides.html:
The original studies compared people's memories of the previous decade with other people's predictions for the next. They did not follow every participant for ten years to verify those forecasts.

Memory and cohort differences could affect the gap. The finding is a reason for humility, not proof that your future tastes must change.

title: Why the surprising rumor outruns the correction
hook: On Twitter, false stories often traveled faster than true ones—and the obvious explanation was incomplete.
author: Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy & Sinan Aral
source_title: The Spread of True and False News Online
summary: A 2018 study tracing approximately 126,000 fact-checked stories on Twitter found that false stories spread farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than true ones. Falsehoods appeared more novel, while bots amplified true and false stories at similar rates.
body: Researchers studied the diffusion of about 126,000 true and false stories tweeted by roughly three million people between 2006 and 2017.
Falsehood traveled farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than truth in the observed cascades; the gap was especially pronounced for political stories.
False stories were more novel by the study's measures, and automated accounts did not explain the relative advantage: bots accelerated both categories at similar rates.
takeaways: What feels surprising is not necessarily what is reliable.
The observed advantage of false stories cannot be attributed simply to bots.
This is evidence about fact-checked Twitter stories in 2006–2017, not every platform or kind of information.
nuance: The study is observational. Novelty and emotional reactions are plausible contributors, not experimentally established causes of the diffusion gap. Its fact-checked sample and historical Twitter setting limit generalization.
application: When a post seems irresistible because it is shocking or new, pause before sharing; inspect its original evidence rather than treating surprise as a credibility signal.

quiz.question: What did the 2018 Twitter diffusion study find about bots?
choices: Bots preferentially spread false stories
Bots accelerated true and false stories at similar rates
The dataset excluded all automated accounts
quiz.explanation: Bots amplified both kinds of stories similarly; the relative spread advantage of false stories was not explained by bots alone.

slides.title: Why does a wild rumor travel so far?
slides.html:
A shocking story appears in your feed. You want to send it to someone before you have even checked it.

In a large study of Twitter, researchers found a troubling pattern: false stories often traveled farther and faster than true ones.

slides.title: Follow the story, not just the tweet
slides.html:
Researchers traced about 126,000 fact-checked stories shared by roughly three million Twitter users from 2006 through 2017.

False stories spread farther, faster, deeper and more broadly in the observed cascades. The difference was particularly pronounced for political news.

left.label: TRUE STORIES
left.title: More limited cascades
left.text: Typically reached fewer people in this dataset.

right.label: FALSE STORIES
right.title: Wider cascades
right.text: Often reached more people through longer sharing chains.

slides.title: It wasn't simply a bot problem
slides.html:
One obvious suspect is automated accounts. But the researchers found that bots accelerated the spread of true and false stories at similar rates.

The relative advantage of falsehood remained. The pattern pointed toward human sharing behavior as an important part of the story.

slides.title: What would you share first?
slides.html: The false stories in the study were also more novel by the researchers' measures. Surprise might help explain why people pass them along, though the study did not prove that novelty caused the gap.

interaction.question: Which reaction is a better reason to verify before sharing?
choices: This is so surprising everyone must see it
I found the original evidence and checked it
Lots of people are reposting it
interaction.feedback: Surprise and popularity are not evidence. Novelty may help a story spread even when it is false.

slides.title: An observed pattern, not a universal law
slides.html:
The researchers analyzed fact-checked stories on Twitter during 2006–2017. Their results do not establish that falsehood always wins on every platform, or prove precisely why people share it.

The practical insight is modest but powerful: when something feels astonishing, that feeling may be a reason to slow down.

title: A placebo can work even when you know it's a placebo
hook: Does a placebo require a doctor to fool you? One randomized trial tested the opposite.
author: Ted J. Kaptchuk and colleagues
source_title: Placebos without Deception: A Randomized Controlled Trial in Irritable Bowel Syndrome
summary: In a small three-week randomized trial involving 80 patients with irritable bowel syndrome, people knowingly taking inert placebo pills reported greater symptom improvement than a no-treatment group receiving similar clinician attention. The finding challenges the idea that placebo responses always require deception, but does not show that inert pills treat underlying disease.
body: The researchers openly explained that the pills contained no active medication, while also describing placebo effects and encouraging regular use.
Eighty patients with irritable bowel syndrome were randomized to these openly labeled placebo pills or no pills; clinician interactions were designed to be comparable.
At three weeks, the placebo group reported better overall improvement and symptom relief on the study's questionnaires. The study was small, short and measured largely self-reported outcomes.
takeaways: Expectations and treatment rituals may influence subjective symptoms without deception.
A placebo comparison must consider clinician attention and the explanation patients receive.
This experiment does not justify replacing effective medical treatment with inert pills.
nuance: The single-center trial had 80 participants, lasted three weeks and used largely patient-reported IBS outcomes. Participants were told that placebo effects can be powerful, so the results do not isolate pill-taking from expectation-setting. It did not establish a physiological cure or generalize to every condition.
application: When reading a health study, separate symptom relief from disease modification, and inspect what the control group experienced—not merely whether a pill contained an active ingredient.

quiz.question: What did the open-label placebo trial actually demonstrate?
choices: People must be deceived for placebo effects to occur
In this small IBS trial, knowingly taking inert pills improved reported symptoms versus a no-pill comparison
Placebo pills cured the underlying cause of IBS
quiz.explanation: Participants knew the pills were inert; the trial found better self-reported IBS outcomes over three weeks, not a demonstrated cure.

slides.title: Would a sugar pill help if you knew the truth?
slides.html:
Imagine a doctor hands you pills and says plainly: these contain no active medicine.

Would taking them be pointless? A 2010 randomized trial asked whether the familiar treatment ritual might still change how people feel—even without deception.

slides.title: Two groups, one unusual prescription
slides.html: Researchers enrolled 80 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Both groups had comparable clinician contact. One group received no pills; the other knowingly took inert pills, with an explanation emphasizing possible placebo effects.

left.label: CONTROL
left.title: No pills
left.text: Comparable clinician interaction, without the pill-taking ritual.

right.label: OPEN-LABEL PLACEBO
right.title: Known inert pills
right.text: Pills clearly labeled placebo, taken regularly after an encouraging explanation.

slides.title: The group that knew still felt better
slides.html:
After three weeks, the open-label placebo group reported greater overall improvement and lower IBS symptom severity than the no-treatment group.

The result challenges a simple assumption: deception is not always necessary for a placebo response. It does not tell us which part of the experience produced the difference.

slides.title: What was bundled with the pills?
slides.html: The pills were inert, but the intervention was not just a chemical-free capsule. It included an explanation, a routine, and a medical context.

interaction.prompt: What additional comparison could help isolate the effect of the pill-taking ritual?
interaction.answer: Compare openly labeled pills with a group receiving the same explanation and attention but no pills. This trial matched clinician contact, but the ritual and expectations were still intertwined.

slides.title: Feeling better is not the same as curing disease
slides.html:
This was one small, short, single-center trial, with outcomes largely based on what patients reported. It did not establish that inert pills reverse underlying pathology or work for every illness.

The useful insight is narrower—and more interesting: expectations, context, and treatment routines may matter even when everyone knows the pill is inactive.

title: Why your coffee mug is worth more once it's yours
kicker: The price tag ownership quietly rewrites
hook: Would you pay as much for a mug as you'd demand to give it up? In a classic experiment, the answers diverged.
author: Daniel Kahneman, Jack L. Knetsch and Richard H. Thaler
source_title: Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem
summary: In classic market experiments, people randomly given coffee mugs typically demanded more to sell them than others offered to buy them. Trading was lower than predicted, whereas markets using tokens with assigned redemption values traded as expected. Ownership can influence valuation, although this is not a universal rule for every good or market.
body: Researchers randomly assigned coffee mugs to some participants and organized markets in which mug owners could sell and others could buy.

The mug markets showed a pronounced gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay, with fewer trades than standard predictions. Parallel markets for induced-value tokens behaved much closer to the theoretical benchmark.
This contrast suggested that the reluctance to trade mugs was not merely a failure to understand the trading procedure.
takeaways: Owning an item can change the price at which you are willing to part with it.
Comparing consumption goods with redeemable tokens helps separate valuation from market mechanics.
A valuation gap in an experiment does not imply that all prices or trades behave this way.
nuance: These were controlled market experiments. Subsequent work has explored when the effect weakens, including with experience and different procedures; the paper does not prove an immutable ownership bias in every context.
application: When selling an old possession, ask what you would pay to acquire the same item today. The gap between that number and your asking price may reveal an attachment to ownership.

quiz.question: Why did the researchers also run markets for tokens with assigned values?
choices: To test whether trading procedures alone caused the low mug-trading volume
To show that every market has identical prices
To prove mugs are objectively worthless
quiz.explanation: Token markets traded near the predicted volume, helping distinguish the mug valuation effect from a generic inability to trade.

slides.title: A mug changes value when it changes hands
slides.html:
Imagine receiving an ordinary coffee mug for free. A stranger offers to buy it. How much would you demand?

Now reverse the situation: you don't own it. How much would you pay?

Economic theory gives us a reason to expect these numbers to be fairly close. Real people often disagree.

slides.title: Same mug. Different side of the deal.
slides.html:
In experiments published in 1990, researchers randomly gave mugs to some participants. Owners could sell; nonowners could buy.

The groups faced the same object, but ownership changed the question they were answering.

left.label: BUYER
left.title: How much to acquire it?
left.text: The highest price you'd willingly pay for a mug you do not own.

right.label: OWNER
right.title: How much to surrender it?
right.text: The lowest price you'd accept to give up the mug you already have.

slides.title: The mugs barely moved
slides.html:
Mug owners typically wanted substantially more than prospective buyers would pay. As a result, fewer mugs traded than the researchers' benchmark predicted.

One interpretation is the endowment effect: possessing something can raise its subjective value, even if you received it by chance.

slides.title: What if trading itself was the problem?
slides.html:
The researchers also ran markets for tokens that could be redeemed for assigned monetary values. Those markets produced trading volumes much closer to predictions.

That contrast mattered: participants could navigate the market, yet consumption goods produced unusually little exchange.

left.label: MUG MARKET
left.title: Undertrading
left.text: Owners' selling prices and buyers' offers diverged.

right.label: TOKEN MARKET
right.title: Near benchmark
right.text: Trade volume was close to the predicted level.

slides.title: Your old headphones
slides.html: Suppose you're asking a surprisingly high price for headphones you no longer use. Before listing them, consider a different question.

interaction.prompt: What would you pay for an identical used pair today?
interaction.answer: If you'd pay far less than you're asking, part of the difference may reflect attachment to what is already yours. Condition and resale hassle can also matter.

slides.title: Not every object behaves like a mug
slides.html:
The experiment reveals a valuation pattern in particular controlled markets. It doesn't prove that ownership always inflates value, or that people cannot learn to trade differently.

The practical insight is a question, not a diagnosis: am I pricing the object—or the feeling of giving it up?

title: The smartest invention may belong to no single inventor
kicker: Why culture can act like shared intelligence
hook: Some tools and techniques are too complicated for one person to reinvent. How does a society keep making them better?
author: Michael Muthukrishna and Joseph Henrich
summary: Muthukrishna and Henrich describe innovation as a process emerging from a network of people who learn from one another, recombine ideas, and accumulate improvements over generations. Their collective-brain framework shifts attention from isolated genius to social learning, connectivity and cumulative culture; it is a theoretical synthesis, not a controlled proof that larger networks always innovate more.
body: An individual rarely invents every component of a complex technology from scratch. Skills, methods and tools can be transmitted socially and improved incrementally.
The collective-brain framework treats innovation as emerging from interactions among learners, inventors and the accumulated knowledge they inherit.
Networks can expand access to useful ideas and allow recombination, but the quality of social learning and the structure of connections matter; sheer population size is not a magic switch.
takeaways: Innovation can be cumulative: each generation starts with discoveries it did not personally make.
The connections between people can be as important as the capabilities of individuals.
Preserving and sharing knowledge is part of the innovation process, not merely a record of it.
nuance: The article develops and synthesizes a theoretical framework with supporting literature; it does not establish a single causal law that bigger groups always create better ideas. Networks can also spread errors, and institutions shape who gets to contribute.
application: When tackling a hard problem, map the knowledge you inherit, seek people with different partial solutions, and document improvements so the next person starts further ahead.

quiz.question: In the collective-brain view, where does much innovation come from?
choices: One exceptional individual working without outside ideas
People learning from, combining and improving ideas across a network and over time
Population size alone, regardless of connections or learning
quiz.explanation: The framework emphasizes social learning, connections, recombination and cumulative improvements rather than isolated genius.

slides.title: Who invented the modern world?
slides.html:
Think of a bicycle, a telescope, or a smartphone. Can you name one person who invented every essential component?

Usually not. Each object combines techniques, materials, and discoveries inherited from many others.

Researchers Michael Muthukrishna and Joseph Henrich offer a useful lens: the collective brain.

slides.title: A chain that remembers
slides.html: A person discovers a useful trick. Someone else learns it, improves it, and passes the better version onward. Over time, the resulting technique may become too intricate for one individual to reconstruct alone.

items.title: Learn
items.text: Inherit tools and know-how from others.

items.title: Transmit
items.text: Pass the improved version to the next learner.

slides.title: From lone genius to connected minds
slides.html:
In their 2016 synthesis, the authors argue that innovation depends not only on clever individuals but also on who can learn from whom and how ideas are preserved.

A breakthrough may be the latest link in a long chain, rather than a lightning bolt from nowhere.

slides.title: Two clever villages
slides.html: Imagine two communities with equally talented makers. One keeps discoveries secret. The other shares successful methods, critiques mistakes, and combines techniques.

interaction.prompt: Which community has a better chance of accumulating improvements—and why?
interaction.answer: The connected community has more opportunities to retain, test and recombine knowledge. That is a prediction of the collective-brain framework, not a guarantee: institutions and incentives still matter.

slides.title: More people isn't a magic formula
slides.html:
This is a theoretical framework supported by a wider research literature, not an experiment proving that any larger network will innovate faster.

Connections can transmit mistakes as well as discoveries. Access, incentives, trust, and institutions affect whether useful knowledge survives.

The lesson is to build learning pathways, not simply bigger crowds.

slides.title: Leave a better starting point
slides.html:
On your next project, ask three questions: What did I inherit? Whose different expertise could improve it? What should I record so someone else can build on it?

Even a concise note, reusable method, or documented failure can be a contribution to a collective brain.
